Replace the per-key finder with a single callback walk (#1522)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

`finder.h` exported a resumable iterator, `finder_t` plus
`finder_init()`,
`find_next()` and `finder_cleanup()`, for walking every entry that
matches one
identity. Nothing needed it to be resumable: both drivers, `getall()`
and the
items view set algebra, collect every match into a list and only then
run a
user `__eq__` against it, because a re-entrant mutation must not happen
mid-walk. What the protocol did cost was a ~4.5 KB struct declared by
each
caller, a "not zero-initialized, cleanup only needs `nvisited_few`"
contract
for each to honour, and a `finder_cleanup()` on every error path;
`finder_collect()` carried a second failure label for that reason alone.

The header becomes `walk.h` and exports one function, `md_walk_key()`,
which
owns the probe walk and the visited-entry bitmap and calls a visitor per
match.
Its two consumers move next to their own callers: `getall()` into
`hashtable.h`
beside `popall()`, and the collect helper into `views.h` above the six
set
operations that use it. The algorithm, the dedup bitmap and the critical
section boundaries are unchanged.

Two small things worth flagging for the reviewer. The version check
moves from
the top of `find_next()` to just after the visitor call, which is the
same
check at the same point in the sequence, since the old consumer loop
called
`find_next()` once more even after the last match. And
`assert(finder->iter.keys == finder->md->keys)` is dropped: it sat
directly
above the `if` that handles exactly that condition, so a debug build
aborted
where a release build correctly raised `RuntimeError`.

`md_walk_key()` keeps `find_next()`'s plain field reads and does not
include
`freethreading.h`, per #1518's rule that reads made under `md`'s
critical
section stay plain.

This touches the C extension only. The pure-Python backend has no
equivalent:
its `getall()` and items view set algebra dedup by marking `entry.hash`
in the
table and restoring it afterwards, over the `iter_hash()` generator,
with no
finder object and no visited bitmap, so there is nothing to mirror.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No behavior change. Keeping the walk's position in registers instead of
reloading it from the finder on every step does make things faster:
`getall()`
on a key with many values by about 30%, `CIMultiDict.getall()` by about
24%,
and `itemsview.isdisjoint()` by about 10%. Everything else measured
within
noise, nothing regressed.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No; it removes a caller-visible contract rather than adding one. A new
consumer
writes a visitor and cannot forget to release the bitmap.

Explain why md_clear() keeps Py_CLEAR() on the GIL build (#1526)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

`md_clear()` holds the last three stores to a shared entry field that do
not go through `_multilib/freethreading.h`. #1518 left them alone on
purpose but recorded the reason only in its own PR footer, so this puts
it
at the site. Nothing else changes.

Keeping the raw access wins on two counts. `Py_CLEAR()` is not a decref
plus `reset_identity()`: it skips the store entirely when the field is
already NULL, which the accessors cannot express. And the block is the
`#else` arm of `#ifdef Py_GIL_DISABLED`, so it compiles only on the GIL
build, where every accessor is plain field access and there is no
ordering
for one to carry; the free-threaded build reaches none of it, since
`_md_retire()` owns that path. A `clear_identity()` would therefore
exist
solely for a single GIL-only call site, which fails the bar #1518 set
for
adding an accessor: it has to unify the two builds.

The two alternatives were built and measured rather than argued about;
the
numbers are in the footer.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No. Both builds compile to byte-identical machine code.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. It is four lines of comment.

Add a public C API capsule, with optional Cython support (#1480)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

Adds a public C API capsule (`multidict._multidict.CAPI`, reached
through `multidict_capi.h` / `multidict_capi_struct.h`) so other C
extensions can create and manipulate `MultiDict`, `CIMultiDict`,
their proxies, and `istr` directly, without going through the
Python-level API. Covers type checks and constructors for all four
mapping types plus `istr`, `getversion()` and `len()`, and
`add()`, `clear()`, `setdefault()`, and single-item access (`in`,
`[]`, `del`, `pop()`) for the mutable types. `GetItem`, `Pop`, and
`SetDefault` follow the `PyDict_GetItemRef` / `PyDict_SetDefaultRef`
design, reporting a missing key through the return code rather than
an exception. `MultiDict_ForEach` visits every item, or just the
items for one key, through a callback, without allocating a list.

The same capsule is also reachable from Cython: `multidict/__init__.pxd`
lets third-party Cython code `cimport multidict`, mirrored by a
`multidict/_testcyapi.pyx` test harness. Cython is optional and never
a real dependency of `multidict` itself; an ordinary or release build
never sees it, and a dedicated CI job exercises the opt-in path.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No behavior change for existing Python-level usage. This adds a new,
opt-in C API surface for other C extensions and Cython code to use.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

The struct only ever grows at the end, so older clients keep working
against newer `multidict` builds. The Cython binding is test-only and
opt-in, so it adds no ongoing dependency burden.

## Related issue number

Supersedes and closes #1183, #1190, #1191 (earlier C API drafts).

Compute the ASCII identity of a CIMultiDict key directly (#1527)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

`_ci_key_to_identity()` called `str.lower()` on every plain `str` key,
so a
`CIMultiDict` paid an attribute lookup, a vectorcall, a string
allocation and
a from-scratch hash on every single lookup, insert and delete. For an
ASCII
string CPython's `str.lower()` is `PyUnicode_New(len, 127)` filled by
`Py_TOLOWER()` per byte, and it has no shortcut for a string that is
already
lowercase, so even `d["content-type"]` allocated and rehashed a copy.

An exact `str` that is ASCII is now handled directly. The key is scanned
for an
uppercase byte, eight at a time, and if it has none it already is its
own
identity, so it is reused as is: no copy, and `_unicode_hash()` finds
the key's
cached `ob_shash` instead of hashing a fresh string. A key that does
have
uppercase is lowered straight into a new string, still without the
method call.

The gate is deliberately `PyUnicode_CheckExact`. A `str` subclass may
override
`lower()`, and the identity of a subclass instance has to keep coming
from the
override; `tests/test_mutable_multidict.py` and
`tests/test_multidict.py`
already depend on that, and there is a new test that pins it. `istr`,
`str`
subclasses and non-ASCII keys all take the path they took before.

Everything below the `istr` check now sits behind a `noinline` call, and
`compiler.h` gains a `NOINLINE` macro alongside `COLD` and
`ALWAYS_INLINE` for
it. This is load-bearing, not cosmetic. `md_calc_identity()` is inlined
into
every `md_*()` that takes a key, so it carries `_ci_key_to_identity()`
with it,
and growing that function pushed `md_contains()` and `md_next()` past
the
inliner's budget at their own call sites. The cost landed on code the
fast path
cannot help: `keys().isdisjoint()` took 31% more instructions on a plain
`MultiDict`, whose keys never reach the case-insensitive branch at all.
Behind
the call, `_ci_key_to_identity()` is smaller than it was before this
change and
the effect is gone.

`multidict/_multidict_py.py` is not touched. The dual-backend rule
applies, but
there is nothing to mirror: the pure Python `_CIMixin._identity()`
already is
`key.lower()`, and no pure-Python spelling of the same idea is cheaper
than the
method call it would replace.

Merge the deferred-decref accumulator into reflist_t (#1530)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

The C extension carried two collectors of strong references that differ
only in how they are drained: `reflist_t` turned them into a list,
`deferred_decref_t` decref'd them. Both exist for the same reason,
that neither job can run while a critical section is held, and both
were filled by an almost identical push. They are now one type in
`_multilib/reflist.h`, built on the deferred accumulator's chain of
blocks, and `deferred_decref.h` is gone.

The inline array that starts the chain is small, 15 slots: it sits in
the caller's stack frame, and a bigger one costs `md_get_all()` its
inlining into the calling method. Everything past it is a 127 slot heap
block, and every path that touches a block is kept out of line, so a
call that never overflows compiles to roughly what the old plain array
did while a call that does overflow stops copying its refs to ever
bigger buffers. `getall()` and `popall()` on keys with many values come
out a few percent ahead; see the numbers below.

Pure Python is untouched: `reflist_t` is a C-side implementation
detail with no counterpart in `_multidict_py.py`.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No. The collected references are still handed back in push order, and
both drains keep the ownership rules they had.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No, it is one header and one push path fewer to keep in sync.

Add a tool for diffing the code the C extension compiles to (#1529)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

Adds `tools/codegen_diff.py`, which reports the functions GCC emits
differently before and after a change to the C extension. It builds
`multidict/_multidict.c` from a baseline ref and from the working tree
against the same interpreter headers, normalizes the fields that move
when code is relocated, and compares function by function.

The normalization is the point, in both directions. Without it a raw
`objdump` diff is unusable, because one instruction-length change shifts
every later label and untouched functions look modified. Normalizing too
much is the opposite failure: immediate operands and memory
displacements are deliberately left alone, so that a store moving to
another structure field is reported rather than folded away. The
disassembly is taken with relocations, because in a relocatable object
the target of an external call lives only in the relocation record.
`--self-test` compiles a pair of sources for each of those and checks
the difference is reported.

What remains is churn that is not a behavior change: a helper that gets
smaller frees inlining budget, and a stack slot that moves changes a
displacement. The report carries the two numbers that separate those
from a real difference, the instruction count and whether the set of
called symbols moved.

`--probe` compiles a caller-supplied translation unit instead of the
extension, which is how a helper that GCC always inlines, and that
therefore has no standalone copy in the object, gets looked at on its
own.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No, it is a development tool. Nothing imports it, nothing in CI runs
it, and it is not packaged.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

It is stdlib Python with no new dependency, and nothing depends on it,
so it can be deleted if it stops earning its place. Two limits are worth
knowing up front: it assumes GCC on x86-64, and it hardcodes `gcc` and
`objdump` rather than honouring `CC`. Teaching it clang would mostly be
a matter of the normalization rules.

## Related issue number

None. The tooling was rebuilt by hand for #1518, #1526 and #1528; this
puts it in the tree instead.

Publish dict versus multidict comparison tables (#1532)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

`docs/benchmark.rst` explained how to run the benchmarks but published
no numbers, so the question a reader arrives with, what `MultiDict`
costs compared with a plain `dict`, went unanswered, and the
free-threaded build's overhead was undocumented. The page now carries
per-operation tables for `dict`, `MultiDict` and `CIMultiDict` on the
GIL build, the same on the free-threaded build, a free-threading
overhead summary with `dict` as the control, and a pure-Python backend
table. Fifteen rows, one per operation the two types share.

The numbers are Callgrind instruction counts rather than wall clock,
because they do not depend on scheduling or CPU frequency and so
reproduce on a busy machine; a regression shows up as a changed integer.
`benchmarks/callgrind_driver.py` measures each cell with four child
processes, two round counts per arm. Differencing two non-zero round
counts cancels interpreter startup, and subtracting an arm with the
operation elided cancels the driving loop, which is worth a few hundred
instructions per iteration and would otherwise compress every ratio
toward 1. `benchmarks/render_tables.py` turns two runs into the tables
and rewrites the block between markers in the page.

Getting there needed the scripts restructured. The pyperf script built
each benchmark out of `exec`'d source templates, which left nowhere to
run setup between measured iterations and limited it to six
non-destructive operations. `benchmarks/operations.py` now holds every
operation as a setup/run/noop triple that all three entry points read,
and the rebuild a destructive operation needs happens in setup, outside
the measured region, so `pop()`, `clear()` and `del d[key]` can be
measured without counting it.

Both backends are covered: the tables carry `MultiDict` and
`CIMultiDict` for the C extension and for the pure-Python
implementation, imported directly from `multidict._multidict` and
`multidict._multidict_py`, so one install measures both.

`AGENTS.md` now asks for the tables to be refreshed in the same PR as
any significant performance change, with the commands to do it.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No. Nothing outside `benchmarks/`, `docs/` and `AGENTS.md` is touched.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

The tables need regenerating when performance moves, which is the point
of them; `AGENTS.md` documents how. The measurement is deterministic, so
it does not need a quiet machine, but it does need Valgrind and one
virtualenv per interpreter build.

## What do these changes do?

The single-key methods took `md`'s critical section in `_multidict.c`
and
`capsule.h`, and only then turned the key into its identity and hashed
it.
That work reads the key plus `md->is_ci` and `md->state`, both fixed for
the
object's lifetime, so it never needed the lock; on a free-threaded build

safepoint and suspends the section anyway.

`getall()` and
`MultiDict_ForEach()` hoist the hash too; the set operators in `views.h`

`threading.RLock` over whole method bodies for a different reason,

bytecode on every build, and this is internal lock granularity with no

Reject arguments passed both positionally and by name (#1545)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

`parse2()` in `_multilib/parser.h` enumerated the shapes the keyword
tuple could take, and the shapes where a keyword repeats an argument
already bound positionally were not among them. The surplus arguments
were dropped rather than rejected, so `md.get("a", "b", key="c")`
quietly returned the value for `"a"`, and `add()` was worse:
`md.add("a", key="k", value="v")` read its value out of the first
keyword slot and stored `("a", "k")`.

The enumeration is replaced by a walk over the keyword tuple that binds
each name and rejects one that is already bound, mirroring how CPython
binds arguments for an equivalent `def`, down to reporting the leftmost
offending keyword. That also corrects the arity messages, whose two
`minargs` labels were swapped: methods with an optional second argument
claimed to take exactly one, and `add()` claimed to take a range.

The two parameter names are distinct, so the walk compares the one still
unbound first. Without that, `get(key, default=...)` pays a second
`PyUnicode_CompareWithASCIIString()`, which measured as +4.3% on that
call; ordering it this way brings it back to +0.87%.

Only the C extension is affected. The pure-Python implementation already
raised `TypeError` for every one of these and is unchanged; it served as
the oracle for the expected messages.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

Yes. Calls that were silently accepted now raise `TypeError`, matching
the pure-Python backend, and `md.add("a", key="k", value="v")` no longer
stores a wrong value. The wording of some existing `TypeError` messages
changed as a result.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. `parse2()` is shorter than it was, and the error precedence follows
one rule instead of a case per keyword-tuple shape.

Pool small hash tables in the module state (#1539)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

`htkeys_new()` and `htkeys_free()` carried a standing TODO to do what
CPython does for `PyDictKeysObject`. They now check a bounded
per-size-class pool held in the module state, which every multidict
reaches through its cached `state` pointer. A miss allocates and a full
pool frees, so the ordinary path is unchanged.

Size classes `log2_size` 3 to 8, at depths 32, 32, 32, 16, 8 and 4:
about 109 KB per interpreter with every pool full. The ladder stops
where a 100-item constructor pre-sizes to, since past that the
allocation is a small part of filling the table.

Nothing is pooled on a free-threaded build, and that was the measurement
that decided the design. A shared pool needs an atomic exchange to pop
and another to push; on x86 an exchange is a locked operation whatever
memory order it asks for, which came to a flat ~41 cycles per round trip
against mimalloc's 30-52, so it lost below a 1456-byte block. mimalloc
already gives every thread its own freelist. On a GIL build the same
pool is ~10 cycles against pymalloc's 26-55 and libc `malloc`'s 117-158.
Instruction counts said the opposite, 22 against 108-312, which is the
blind spot: callgrind cannot see what a locked exchange costs.

The pools live in the module state rather than at file scope because
under a per-interpreter GIL a block has to be freed by the interpreter
that allocated it. They hold no reference, so `module_traverse()` needs
no change; `module_clear()` drains them.

`MULTIDICT_NO_FREELIST=1` builds without them. A pooled block never
reaches `free()`, so AddressSanitizer can neither poison it nor report a
use-after-free on it, and an ASan run now wants a second pass with that
set. AGENTS.md says so.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No. Faster construction and teardown, nothing observable otherwise.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. The pool is one small header, and it degrades to the present
behaviour: an empty pool allocates, a full one frees, and a pool that
was never given a capacity misses every time.

## Related issue number

None. This is the TODO that stood in `htkeys.h` at `htkeys_new()` and
`htkeys_free()`.

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

Three changes to the argument handling of the C extension, no behaviour
change in any of them.

`parse2()` compiled to a single outlined clone shared by all eleven call
sites and was inlined nowhere, so `md.get(key)` paid a call into the
keyword machinery it never used. The all-positional case now binds in
the inline wrapper, five instructions at the call site, and the rest
moved to a `COLD parse2_slow()`. Since the keyword walk is out of line
anyway, it takes the tuple through `PyTuple_GET_SIZE()` and
`PyTuple_GET_ITEM()`; all eleven methods are
`METH_FASTCALL | METH_KEYWORDS`, so `kwnames` is a tuple or `NULL` and
the error branches of the checked calls were unreachable.

Parameter names are now interned in the module state and matched against
`kwnames` by identity before falling back to a comparison, which is what
`find_keyword()` in CPython's `Python/getargs.c` does. A call written as
`get(key=k)` settles on a pointer compare; the `memcmp()` it replaces
was
45% of the keyword path. The fallback is not optional: `get(**{"key":
k})`
builds names that never reach the intern table, and there is a test for
exactly that.

call and carried a flag to release it again, although it is only
reachable when the key is absent. It now does the lookup directly and
produces the constant on the miss path, where it is the return value.
`setdefault()` keeps the old shape, since it has to hand the default to
`md_set_default()` inside the critical section.

Skip zeroing hash table entries that are about to be overwritten (#1540)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

Two places built a table's entries array twice over.

`md_clone_from_ht()` allocated with a raw `PyMem_Malloc()` and then
memcpy'd the source over every byte, so it neither used the pool nor
needed the initialisation `htkeys_new()` would have done. It now takes
uninitialised storage from the same pool, which skips both memsets.

`_md_resize()` allocated a zeroed entries array and then wrote the front
of it from the old table, so everything it copied had just been zeroed
for nothing. The new table now comes back untouched and only the part
past the copy is zeroed. The count comes from the copy itself rather
than from `md->used`: the two agree, and there is an assert saying so,
but taking it from the copy means a table can never be published over
entries nothing has written, which `ASSERT_CONSISTENT()` would read.

Neither memset can simply be shortened to the used prefix instead.
`_md_resize()` zeroes `oldkeys->nentries` before retiring while the
entries still hold stale non-owning pointers, so a table arriving at
`_md_free_retired()` from a resize reports no dirty entries and has
them; and `ASSERT_CONSISTENT()` reads every entry a table has room for,
not just the used prefix.

The resize half needs no pool and is the only part that moves on a
free-threaded build.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No. Faster copying and resizing, nothing observable otherwise.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. The byte count of a table is now derived in one place,
`htkeys_alloc_size()`, from `log2_size` alone, with `htkeys_sizeof()`
reading the same number back off an existing table under an assert that
the two agree.

Skip the retired-table drain when nothing is retired (#1546)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

On the free-threaded build every lock-free reader that brings
`num_active_readers` back to zero calls `_md_drain_retired()`, which
without a second thread is every single lookup. The first thing that
function does is a sequentially consistent exchange on `md->retired`,
and that list is empty almost every time.

The drain now checks the list with a load first and the rest of it sits
behind a call, so a lookup with nothing to free pays one load instead of
an out-of-line call and a read-modify-write. The load stays sequentially
consistent: a writer that pushes and then reads `num_active_readers` as
nonzero leaves the table for whoever brings that count to zero, so the
reader doing so must not be able to miss the push, and only a seq_cst
load is ordered against the push in the single total order. On x86-64
that is the same plain `mov`, so it is free; the cost being skipped is
the exchange.

Instructions per operation, CPython 3.14.7 free-threaded:

| Operation | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `key in md` | 283 | 253 (-10.6%) |
| `md[key]` | 317 | 292 (-7.9%) |
| `md.get(key)`, miss | 499 | 474 (-5.0%) |

`CIMultiDict` moves -8.1%, -6.2% and -3.3% on the same three. No other
benchmarked operation changes beyond the measurement's noise floor.
Wall clock improves more than the instruction counts do, because
Callgrind cannot see the removed `lock`-prefixed exchange. Measured back
to back against a build of the merge base, two passes each: `key in md`
35.5/35.3 ns before against 29.0/28.7 after, `md[key]` 37.1/36.9 against
30.9/30.6, so about -18%. `CIMultiDict` moves within the noise of this
machine on wall clock and I would not claim a figure for it.

This is free-threaded only. `atomic_helpers.h` is entirely inside
`#ifdef Py_GIL_DISABLED`, and `tools/codegen_diff.py` reports `0 of 190
functions differ` for the GIL build. It is also C-extension only: the
pure-Python backend has no table retirement to skip.

The second commit regenerates `docs/benchmark.rst`. Those numbers were
last collected on the branch of #1532, so the refresh also absorbs
#1533 through #1538; the free-threaded read rows are the part this
change accounts for.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No, other than free-threaded reads being faster.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. The retirement protocol is unchanged; one branch is added in front
of it, and the reasoning for why the window is safe is in the comment
above the gate.

Pool the view and iterator shells (#1541)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

Every `.items()`, `.keys()`, `.values()` and `iter()` allocated a GC
object and dropped it again a moment later. Those shells now come from
two more module-state pools, one for the three view types and one for
the three iterator types: within a family the types differ only in their
methods, so one shell fits any of them, which is the only thing that
makes sharing a pool safe.

A pooled shell keeps the GC preheader it was allocated with, which
`PyObject_GC_UnTrack()` leaves in the untracked state, so reuse only has
to redo what `PyObject_GC_New()` does to the object header. That is left
to `PyObject_Init()` rather than written out, so a debug interpreter's
refcount totals stay right. An interpreter built `--with-trace-refs`
turns the pools off instead, for the reason it cannot have freelists at
all: a shell is reused without ever being freed, so it is never taken
off the all-objects list that reusing it would put it back on.

The pool is reached through the view's multidict, so a shell the GC has
already cleared is freed rather than pooled.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No. Views and iterators are cheaper to make, nothing observable
otherwise.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. It is two more pools of the kind #1539 introduced, and the
`tp_free` path is still there for every shell a pool declines.

Pass the entry identity to the ForEach visitor (#1552)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

The `ForEach` visitor received the key and the value but not the
identity,
the canonical key a multidict actually looks entries up by. On a
`CIMultiDict` that is the internal lower-cased form, so a visitor
wanting
to group or compare entries by it had to derive it again itself,
duplicating work the walk had already done.

`MultiDict_ItemVisitor` now takes
`(void *user_data, PyObject *identity, PyObject *key, PyObject *value)`.
`user_data` stays first so existing call sites keep their shape, and the
identity goes next to the key and value it belongs with rather than at
the
end. `MultiDict_CyItemVisitor` gains it in the same position, keeping
its
own `user_data`-last order. The internal `md_item_visitor_t` in
`_multilib/walk.h` is widened to match, along with `md_walk_all`,
`md_walk_with_hash` and their two in-tree visitors.

The two walks source it differently. `md_walk_with_hash` passes the
identity it was already handed, which every matched entry compares equal
to by the walk's own predicate, so the keyed path does no extra work.
`md_walk_all` reads `entry->identity` and holds a reference across the
visitor call, the same way it already does for the value, since
`_md_ensure_key()` and the visitor can both run Python code that frees
the entry.

The capsule is unreleased: it landed in #1480, after v6.9.1, and
`MultiDict_CAPI_VERSION` is still 1, so no client can have been built
against the narrower signature. That is why the typedef changes in place
instead of growing a parallel entry point at the end of the struct with
a
version bump.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No, for Python-level users. A C or Cython client of the capsule has to
take the extra parameter, but the capsule has not shipped in a release
yet, so there is nothing to migrate.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. Both walks already have the identity in hand, so the wider signature
costs nothing on the keyed path and one reference pair per entry on the
all-entries path.

One benchmark row does move, and it is worth a reviewer's attention.
`d.pop(key)` gets slower on GIL builds: measured on `CPython 3.14.7`,
MultiDict 428.8 to 441.5 instructions (+2.96%) and CIMultiDict 713.5 to
726.2 (+1.78%). Every other row is bit-identical, and the free-threaded
build is unaffected. The cause is not the walk; it is GCC's inlining
budget in `hashtable.h`. Widening `_md_getall_visit` by one parameter is
enough to tip `htkeysiter_init` out of line inside `md_pop_one`, which
`objdump` confirms as a new `call <htkeysiter_init>` on the GIL build
and
not on the free-threaded one.

An `ALWAYS_INLINE` on `htkeysiter_init` removes it, and wins well beyond
`pop` because GCC already outlines that helper in several places on
master. That belongs in its own pull request, with its own numbers, and
is left out of this one deliberately.

`docs/benchmark.rst` is not regenerated here on purpose. The `dict`
control rows in this environment reproduce the committed tables exactly
on both builds (`d.pop(key)` 476.4 against a published 476 on the GIL
build, 587.4 against 587 free-threaded), but every `multidict` row
differs by a few percent (446 published against 428.8 measured on the
GIL build, 562 against 548.8 free-threaded). The interpreter matches
and the compiler does not, so regenerating would rewrite every
`multidict` row for toolchain reasons unrelated to this change. Calling
the one moved row out in prose seemed better than that.

Keep the implicit None default of setdefault() in the module state (#1553)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

`setdefault()` called without an explicit default built the implicit
`None` on every call, then carried a flag to release it again, although
only the call that actually inserts consumes it. `md_set_default()` now
reads a `NULL` *value* as `None`, so the method simply forwards what it
parsed and the flag, its branch and the `Py_CLEAR()` all go away.

The constant lives in the module state rather than coming from
`Py_GetConstant()` at the point of use, because the substitution happens
just before the critical section is taken. On 3.13+ either would do; on
3.10 to 3.12 the `pythoncapi_compat` shim initialises its table lazily
and calls `PyLong_FromLong()`, so a first call landing under the lock
could collect.

Instruction counts against `cd92a6c`, callgrind, 200k calls:

| case | master | this branch | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `d.setdefault(key)`, present key | 491,825,979 | 486,878,820 | -1.01%
|
| `d.setdefault(key, default)`, present key | 494,626,107 | 493,681,201
| -0.19% |
| `d.setdefault(key)`, inserting | 290,700,236 | 290,812,020 | +0.04% |

The inserting call is unchanged, as expected: it still stores the same
constant, just one that was not built for the occasion.

Only the C extension is touched; the pure-Python implementation is
unchanged.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

Not at the Python level; `setdefault()` returns and stores exactly what
it did before.

The public C API gains a little: `MultiDict_SetDefault()` forwards
straight to `md_set_default()`, so it now accepts `NULL` for
*default_value* and reads it as `None`, where the documentation
previously called the argument required. `docs/capi.rst` says so, and
both `_testcapi.c` and `_testcyapi.pyx` exercise it.

`MultiDict_CAPI_VERSION` stays at 1 deliberately. It exists to stop a
client built against a newer header from running on an older runtime,
and version 1 has not shipped: the capsule landed after v6.9.1, so there
is no released runtime that would reject a `NULL` default. Bumping would
announce a boundary no client can be on the wrong side of.

The Cython wrapper cannot express a `NULL` object, but passing `None` is
read identically, so `default_value` just gained a `None` default, which
incidentally makes its signature match the Python method.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. It removes a local variable and a branch from the method, adds one
field to the module state next to the interned names already there, and
leaves `md_set_default()`'s behaviour for a non-`NULL` default
untouched.

Pool the multidict and proxy shells (#1542)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

The last of the short-lived allocations: constructing a `MultiDict`,
`CIMultiDict` or either proxy went through `PyType_GenericAlloc()` every
time. Those shells now come from two more module-state pools, one shared
by `MultiDict` and `CIMultiDict`, which share a struct and differ only
in `md->is_ci`, and one by the two proxy types.

Only the exact types. A subclass has its own basicsize, and possibly its
own `__dict__` and `__weakref__` preheader, so `_md_pool_for()` returns
NULL for one and it keeps going through `tp_alloc`, both when allocating
and when being freed. The `tp_alloc` and `tp_free` slots are untouched.

Reuse redoes what `PyType_GenericAlloc()` does, less the allocation: the
body is zeroed and `PyObject_Init()` sets the header. The preheader
needs nothing, since `PyObject_GC_UnTrack()` leaves the GC header
untracked and `PyObject_ClearWeakRefs()` leaves the managed weakref slot
NULL. A proxy reaches the pool through the multidict it proxies, so one
the GC has already cleared is freed rather than pooled.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No. Construction is cheaper, nothing observable otherwise. Subclasses
are explicitly unaffected, and there is a test for that.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No, though it is the sharpest of the four pools, since it is the one
that has to get the exact-type gate right at both ends. The tests cover
subclasses, weakrefs, proxies, the shared `MultiDict`/`CIMultiDict` pool
not leaking a case-insensitive flag, and shells the collector clears.

Pass the entry identity's hash to the ForEach visitor (#1561)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

The `ForEach` visitor gained the entry's identity in #1552, but not
the hash the mapping stores alongside it. A visitor that buckets or
groups entries by identity therefore had to hash it again, work both
walks had already done.

`MultiDict_ItemVisitor` now takes
`(void *user_data, PyObject *identity, Py_hash_t hash, PyObject *key,
PyObject *value)`, with the hash next to the identity it belongs to.
`MultiDict_CyItemVisitor` gains it in the same position, keeping its
own `user_data`-last order. The internal `md_item_visitor_t` in
`_multilib/walk.h` is widened to match, along with `md_walk_all`,
`md_walk_with_hash` and their two in-tree visitors.

`md_walk_with_hash` passes the hash it was already handed; every
matched entry's own `entry->hash` equals it, since that is the first
half of the walk's match predicate. `md_walk_all` reads `entry->hash`
before the visitor call, alongside the identity and value it already
reads there, since `_md_ensure_key()` and the visitor can both run
Python code that frees the entry.

The capsule is unreleased: it landed in #1480, after v6.9.1, and
`MultiDict_CAPI_VERSION` is still 1, so no client can have been built
against the narrower signature. That is why the typedef changes in
place instead of growing a parallel entry point at the end of the
struct with a version bump.

No, for Python-level users. A C or Cython client of the capsule has to
take the extra parameter, but the capsule has not shipped in a release
yet, so there is nothing to migrate.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. Both walks have the hash in hand already, so the wider signature
costs neither a lookup nor a reference.

Drain the retired hash tables when a cleared multidict is deallocated (#1562)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

On the free-threaded build, `md_clear()` returned early once `md->keys`
was
`&empty_htkeys`, so nothing on that path drained `md->retired`. The
drain
leaves a table on that list whenever it finds a lock-free reader in
flight,
for the next drain to free, and the only drain sites are reader exits
and
retirements; a multidict dropped right after a `clear()` that left its
table
there gets neither, so the table, and the references its entries still
owned,
were never freed. Draining in that early return makes the object's own
teardown the last drain, and that drain does free the table: a lock-free
reader reaches a multidict through a live reference, so its count is
zero by
the time the refcount is.

Getting a table onto that list and leaving it there needs the coarse
active-readers gate to flip between the two times
`_md_drain_retired_slow()`
reads it. The first read sees zero and takes the list, a reader then
enters,
the second read sees it, so the table goes to the push-back at the end
of the
function, and that reader's own exit drain runs before the push-back
lands and
finds the list empty. Nothing is left to drain, and since #1542 the
shell the
object is recycled into is memset, so the next owner cannot pick the
table up
either. Forcing that ordering takes an artificially widened window; the
recipe
and the resulting trace are in the footer.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No, beyond the leak going away. The fix is C-extension only, and only
the
free-threaded build has a retirement scheme; builds with the GIL enabled
emit
byte-identical code.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. It is one load on a path that is not hot, and no benchmarked
operation
moves.

## Related issue number

Fixes #1555

Retry the retired-table drain after pushing tables back (#1565)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

On the free-threaded build, a drain that reads the active-readers gate
as
nonzero pushes the tables it holds back onto `md->retired` and leaves
them to
the reader the gate showed it. That reader can have run its own drain
already,
between `_md_drain_retired_slow()`'s exchange and its push-back, and
found the
list empty; nothing is then left to free those tables. They sit there
until
the multidict is next used, and if it is dropped instead, the references
their
entries own are never released. Rereading the gate after the push-back
tells
the two apart: nonzero means the reader it sees decrements after that
read,
hence after the push-back, so its own drain observes the tables, while
zero
means nothing else will and another pass is what frees them.

This is the window #1555 was reached through, so it is an alternative
fix for
that leak as well as a fix for tables sitting on the list longer than
they
should. It is complementary to #1562 rather than a replacement: this
closes
the window, #1562 backstops the invariant at teardown whatever the drain
does,
and the two do not conflict.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No, other than retired tables being freed when they should be. C
extension
only; the pure-Python implementation has no retirement scheme. Builds
with the
GIL enabled emit byte-identical code.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. One reread of an atomic already being read on that path, on a branch
taken
only when a drain finds a reader in flight.

Refs #1555

Report the entries of retired tables to the collector (#1566)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

On the free-threaded build, a table the drain leaves on `md->retired`
still
owns its entries' references, and `md_traverse()` reported the entries
of
`md->keys` only. A reference cycle running through one of those entries
was
therefore invisible to the collector, which read the values as reachable
from
outside the cycle and kept the whole thing alive; and since a multidict
in a
cycle is only ever freed by the collector, nothing later released them
either.
Reporting those entries is what lets the cycle be collected.

Nothing is reported twice, which is the direction that would be unsafe:
`_md_resize()` zeroes the old table's `nentries` when it hands ownership
to the
new table, so only `md_clear()` retires a table with entries left in it,
and
`md->keys` is empty by then. The walk takes no lock, like the walk of
`md->keys` beside it, and must not: the collector calls `tp_traverse`
with the
world stopped, and a stopped thread can hold any lock this would take.

Stacked on #1562, whose first two commits are included here: reporting
the
references is what lets the collector reach `tp_clear()`, and the drain
#1562
adds there is what releases them. Either alone leaves the cycle
uncollected.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

`gc.get_referents()` on a multidict now lists what a retired table
holds, and
cycles through such an entry become collectable. C extension only; the
pure-Python implementation has no retirement scheme, and the interpreter
traverses its containers itself. Builds with the GIL enabled emit
byte-identical code.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. It is a walk of a list that is almost always empty, on a path the
collector calls.

## Related issue number

Refs #1555

Drop the trailing tombstones when popitem() removes the last entry (#1568)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

`popitem()` in the C extension finds the last live entry by walking
back from `nentries` over the tombstones that earlier deletes left
behind, but never shortened `nentries` afterwards, so each call walked
every entry the previous calls had already removed and popping a
mapping empty cost quadratic time. `md_pop_item()` now sets `nentries`
to the popped entry's position, dropping it and the tombstones after
it, which is what CPython's `dict.popitem()` does and what the
pure-Python implementation already did with `del entries[pos:]`.

The trim is done before the delete releases its references: a `__del__`
on the popped key can re-enter the mapping (on the free-threaded build
by suspending the critical section) and an `add()` from there must land
at the trimmed position, not past it. A test covers that with a `str`
subclass key whose finalizer adds to the mapping, which on a
`CIMultiDict` is released inside `popitem()` because the returned key
is a fresh `istr`.

## What do these changes do?

`CIMultiDict` and `CIMultiDictProxy` had no `Py_tp_methods` slot of
their own, so their method descriptors were the ones inherited from
`MultiDict` and `MultiDictProxy`: `CIMultiDict.get.__objclass__ is

path (`method_vectorcall_*`, `_Py_CheckFunctionResult`, the stack-ref

Recycle the items iterator's result tuple (#1569)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

The C items iterator built a fresh two-tuple on every step with
`PyTuple_Pack()`, and the caller freed it a moment later: the tuple
allocation, its deallocation and the freelist bookkeeping were about
220 of the 380 instructions a step of `for k, v in d.items()` cost,
against 88 for `dict`. The iterator now owns one result tuple, created
with it, and, when the caller has already dropped it (checked with
`PyUnstable_Object_IsUniquelyReferenced()`, which
`pythoncapi_compat.h` provides on every supported version), stores the
next pair into it and returns it again, the way
`dictiter_iternextitem()`
does. A tuple the caller still holds is left alone and a fresh one is
returned instead. The field is never replaced after creation: on the
free-threaded build the uniqueness check is only ever true for the
thread that owns the tuple, so two threads sharing one iterator either
reuse from the owner or allocate, and neither can free the tuple under
the other. The tuple is re-tracked by the collector when reused, since
the collector may have untracked it while it held only atomic items,
and on 3.14 and later its cached hash is reset.

`keys()` and `values()` iterators do not touch the new field. The
pooled iterator shells release the tuple before going back to the pool,
and `tp_traverse` and `tp_clear` cover it.

Only the C extension changes; the pure-Python iterator yields a fresh
tuple each step, and the new test passes on both.

Instruction counts per step of `for k, v in d.items()` over 200 items,
`benchmarks/callgrind_driver.py`, CPython 3.14.7, `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`:

| `for k, v in d.items()` | before | after | | `dict` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `MultiDict`, GIL | 378 | 132 | -65% | 88 |
| `CIMultiDict`, GIL | 382 | 136 | -64% | |
| `MultiDict`, free-threaded | 486 | 224 | -54% | 114 |
| `CIMultiDict`, free-threaded | 490 | 227 | -54% | |

`iter(d.items())` pays for creating the tuple up front, and `iter(d)`
4 instructions for initialising the field; nothing else moves.

Wall clock, interleaved before/after runs pinned to a P-core on an idle
machine, median ns per step:

| `for k, v in d.items()` | before | after | | `dict` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `MultiDict`, GIL | 35.7 | 18.3 | -49% | 14.6 |
| `CIMultiDict`, GIL | 34.5 | 18.2 | -47% | |
| `MultiDict`, free-threaded | 55.8 | 34.5 | -38% | 22.9 |
| `CIMultiDict`, free-threaded | 55.4 | 34.5 | -38% | |

Seven interleaved runs of each build per row, median; the `dict`
column ran alongside as a control and moved under 3%.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No. Code that keeps a tuple sees the same pairs as before; the only
observable difference is that `next(it) is next(it)` can now be true
when the first result was dropped, which is already true of `dict`.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. One field on the iterator, mirrored from CPython's own iterator,
with the pool and GC hooks updated to match. Besides the two tests on
held tuples and the hash cache, a free-threaded stress test pulls from
one items iterator on two threads at once.

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

On the free-threaded build `d[key]`, `d.get()`, `d.getone()` and
`key in d` probe the table without the critical section, and for every
entry on the probe chain took a reference to the entry's identity with
`try_get_ref()` (an atomic load, a `TryIncRef`, a re-load and a

treat an identity that is the very same object as the one being looked

anything else. Only an identity that is a different object still goes

Add a watchers C API (#1551)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

Add a watchers C API, so another C extension can be notified when a
`MultiDict` or `CIMultiDict` changes. It follows CPython's
`PyDict_AddWatcher` family, with two deliberate differences.

The callback gets **two context pointers**: `watcher_data`, fixed when
the
callback is registered, and `user_data`, belonging to one watched
multidict. That is the point of the API: one registered callback can
serve
any number of multidicts and still know, on every event, what owns the
one
that changed. CPython does not need this because its dict watchers are
static functions inside the interpreter.

Events are **delivered after the operation finishes**, not mid-mutation.
Several of the update paths run with the table deliberately inconsistent
(`_md_del_at_for_upd_deferred` leaves an entry half-deleted but still
reachable until `md_post_update` sweeps it, and
`_md_replace`/`_md_update`
carry a `reflist_t` of not-yet-decref'd objects), so calling out to a
client there is the shape behind #1469 and #1489. Events are recorded
into
a per-multidict log instead, which only allocates, and delivered once
the
critical section is released.

The events are multi-value aware, since `add()` on a key that is already
present is an append rather than a modification, and one `__setitem__`
can
both replace a pair and delete several. Each event that concerns a key
carries the identity alongside it, already lowercased for a
`CIMultiDict`,
so a watcher matching `"content-length"` needs no `lower()` of its own,
and
the identity's hash with it, so a watcher keeping its own table does not
have to hash the key again.

C-extension only, like the rest of the capsule API: `_multidict_py.py`
and
`_abc.py` are untouched, and `tests/test_capi.py` skips on the
pure-Python
leg as it already does.

`MultiDict_CAPI_VERSION` stays at 1: version 1 has not shipped, since
7.0
is unreleased, so no client can exist that was built against a capsule
without these entry points.

One thing a reviewer may want to overrule:

- `MultiDictObject` grows one pointer, `md_watch_t *watch`, NULL until
the
first `MultiDict_Watch()`. `tp_basicsize` goes 56 to 64 on GIL 3.12+, 64
  to 72 on 3.10/3.11 and 88 to 96 free-threaded, but what the allocator
  reserves is what actually costs. Measured as RSS over a million empty
  multidicts:

  | build | `tp_basicsize` | bytes per instance |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 3.10.17 | 64 -> 72 | 80.4 -> 96.4 |
  | 3.11.13 | 64 -> 72 | 80.4 -> 96.2 |
  | 3.13.2 | 56 -> 64 | 96.2 -> 96.4 |
  | 3.14.7t | 88 -> 96 | 112.1 -> 112.1 |

  So only 3.10 and 3.11 pay, and they pay 16 rather than 8: pymalloc's
  size classes are 16 bytes apart, and those are the versions that still
  carry an explicit `weaklist` pointer, which puts the object on a class
  boundary. Everywhere else the rounding absorbs it.

  The alternative (an occupancy bitmask in the existing padding after
`is_ci`, which is free, plus a side table in `mod_state`) saves those 16
bytes on two versions, at the price of a keyed lookup at every recording
  site and, on free-threaded builds, a lock over globally shared state
  taken inside the per-object critical section.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

No. Nothing fires until a client registers a watcher and watches a
multidict, and no Python-level API changes.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

The four entry points are small and the event set is fixed. The ongoing
cost is that every new mutation path has to record its events; a debug
build asserts the log is empty at dealloc, which catches a missed flush.

Make the underscore prefix mark header-local helpers in _multilib (#1571)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

Renames the helpers in the `_multilib` headers so that a leading
underscore means exactly "used only within this header". Helpers called
from another header or from `_multidict.c` lose the underscore
(`_md_ensure_key`, `_unicode_hash`, `_str_cmp`, `_update_marks_sync`,
...), and helpers used only in their own header gain one
(`_htkeys_mask`, `_name_is`, `_raise_*`, `_capsule_free`, the
`*1`/`*2`/`*_impl` set operation workers in `views.h`, ...).
`_md_reserve` becomes `md_reserve_for_upd`, since `md_reserve` is
already taken by its wrapper.

Type slots and method callbacks referenced from `PyType_Slot` /
`PyMethodDef` tables keep their names. `GROWTH_RATE` is left as is
(`_GROWTH_RATE` would be a reserved identifier), and so is the unused
`reflist_size()`. Pure rename, no C-level behaviour change; the

Raise the watcher limit from 8 to 32 (#1574)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

Raises `MULTIDICT_MAX_WATCHERS` from 8 to 32. The occupancy mask becomes
a `uint32_t`.

Two changes keep the higher limit from costing anything:

- Delivery walks only the set bits of the mask, using ctz. Previously it
scanned every slot and copied the whole `user_data` array once per
event, which would have made each event cost more at 32 slots.

the multidict's critical section or in dealloc, so moving the record is
safe. `md_watch_detach` now ignores an ID beyond the record.

C extension only; the watchers API has no pure-Python counterpart.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

Up to 32 watchers can be registered at a time instead of 8. Watchers are
not in a release yet, so nothing shipped changes.

Bound the table size a length hint can reserve (#1577)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

Hardens the C extension's size arithmetic against an object whose
`__length_hint__()` reports close to `sys.maxsize`.

`md_reserve_for_upd()` computed `(extra_size + used) * 3 + 1` without an
overflow check, and `_md_resize()` only rejected sizes of 64 bits or
more. A size of 2**61 to 2**63 still passed, and `_htkeys_alloc_size()`
then shifted `1` by 64 or 65. Under `MULTIDICT_ASAN_BUILD=1` that aborts
with `shift exponent 65 is too large for 64-bit type`; on a release
build it happened to end in `MemoryError`. Separately,
`_multidict_extend_parse_args()` added the keyword count to the hint,
wrapped negative, and `extend()`/`update()`/`merge()` returned NULL with
no exception set (`SystemError`).

The fix saturates the keyword addition, ignores a hint too large to
estimate for (as `list.extend()` does when size plus hint overflows),
and adds `htkeys_size_fits()` so `_md_resize()` rejects any size whose
byte count does not fit in `Py_ssize_t`, before any shift happens. The
pure-Python backend does no such arithmetic and is unchanged.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

A `__length_hint__()` too large to estimate for is ignored instead of
raising `MemoryError`, and passing keyword arguments alongside it no
longer raises `SystemError`.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. One comparison on the reserve path and a helper on the resize path,
which is already cold.

Make watcher registration thread safe and retire stale watch bits (#1583)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

`MultiDict_AddWatcher()` and `MultiDict_ClearWatcher()` wrote the
module-wide slot table with plain stores, while event delivery on
another thread read it with no lock. On the free-threaded build that is
a data race, and TSan reports it at `watch.h` against both functions.
Registration now serializes on a `PyMutex` and publishes through new
`freethreading.h` accessors, following CPython's `PyDict_AddWatcher()`.
Delivery stays lock-free.

`ClearWatcher()` also bumps a per-slot generation, and each watch
records the generation it was attached under. A multidict left watched
through a cleared ID used to report to the next registration under that
ID, passing the old registration's `user_data`. That bit is now ignored
until the multidict is watched again. CPython's dict watchers still have
the same reuse hazard; the heap-allocated per-multidict record makes it
cheap to close here. This only affects the C extension: watchers are a C
API feature and have no pure-Python counterpart.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

Yes, for C API clients only. Both registration functions are now safe to
call from any thread, and a cleared watcher's leftover watches no longer
reach a later registration that reuses its ID. The docs drop the warning
about that reuse.

Name the event and multidict when a watcher callback fails (#1585)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

A failing watcher callback is now reported the way CPython's
`_PyDict_SendEvent()` reports a failing dict watcher. The message names
the event and the multidict's type and address, for example `Exception
ignored in MultiDict_EVENT_ADDED watcher callback for
<multidict._multidict.MultiDict object at 0x...>`, and the multidict
itself is no longer passed to `sys.unraisablehook`. Previously every
event except DEALLOCATED passed the multidict, so the default hook would
`repr()` it and could run arbitrary code (a subclass `__repr__`) while
an error was being reported.

On 3.13+ this uses `PyErr_FormatUnraisable()`. On 3.10 to 3.12, which
lack it, it uses `_PyErr_WriteUnraisableMsg()`, and the address is
formatted with `PRIxPTR` because MSVC's `%p` omits the `0x`. This only
affects the C extension: watchers have no pure-Python counterpart.

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

Yes, for C API clients whose watcher callbacks fail:
`sys.unraisablehook` now receives `object=None` and a descriptive
`err_msg`.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No. It is one cold function with a version branch.

Reserve version numbers in per-thread batches on free-threaded builds (#1587)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

On the free-threaded build every mutation bumped one counter shared by
every multidict with an atomic fetch-add. Threads mutating their own,
unrelated multidicts still fought over that one cache line, and with six
threads a `d[key] = value` spent about three quarters of its time there.

Each thread now reserves 256 versions at a time from a process-wide
counter and hands them out from thread-local storage, the same scheme
free-threaded CPython uses for its dict version tags. Versions stay
unique across all multidicts and keep increasing within a thread, but
are no longer ordered across threads; `getversion()` is documented as
equality-only and the C code only ever compares with `!=`. The counter
moved out of module state so a batch left over in a thread can never
overlap a newer module state's range. The thread-locals use the default
TLS model: initial-exec would save a few ns per mutation, but it draws
on glibc's small static TLS reserve for `dlopen()`, and when that is
exhausted the import fails and multidict silently falls back to pure
Python. The GIL build is unchanged, and the pure-Python implementation
has no equivalent contention to fix.

Wall clock, 3.14.7t, ns per mutation, each thread on its own dict and
keys, pinned to separate P-cores, median of 5 interleaved rounds:

| op | threads | master | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `d[k] = v` | 1 | 46.1 | 46.2 |
| `d[k] = v` | 2 | 90.7 | 49.5 |
| `d[k] = v` | 4 | 162.3 | 55.9 |
| `d[k] = v` | 6 | 266.4 | 61.7 |
| `add` + `del` | 1 | 53.3 | 51.0 |
| `add` + `del` | 6 | 288.5 | 74.1 |
| `get()` (control) | 6 | 59.1 | 58.0 |

## Are there changes in behavior for the user?

Faster concurrent mutation on free-threaded builds. Versions from
different threads are no longer ordered relative to each other, which
was never part of the documented contract.

## Is it a substantial burden for the maintainers to support this?

No, it is about thirty lines confined to `next_version()` and a
`THREAD_LOCAL` macro.

Document a cache-invalidating watcher in the C API docs (#1586)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

Adds an "Invalidating a cache" example to `docs/capi.rst`, after the
existing watcher example. It shows the pattern CPython's JIT uses for a
module's globals: the callback clears the cache and unwatches itself,
the next rebuild watches again, and after a fixed number of rebuild
attempts the cache stops trying on a multidict that keeps changing.

An event goes to whoever is watching when the operation finishes, so it
can reach a rebuild that already saw its change, under the GIL too once
`parse()` runs Python code. The cache therefore records the version it
was built from: the callback discards only a cache the multidict has
moved past, and never unwatches while a rebuild owns the watch. On the
free-threaded build the fields also need a lock, which sits behind
`Py_GIL_DISABLED`, so one source serves both builds and works back to
3.10. Bare BATCH brackets are ignored, and a failed parse stops
listening.

Make istr a final class to prevent identity invariant violations (#1573)

## What does this PR do?

Fixes #1535.

As suggested by maintainer @asvetlov, this PR makes `istr` a final class
to disallow subclassing in both the C extension and pure-Python
implementations, preventing canonical identity invariant violations:
- In debug builds of the C extension (`MULTIDICT_DEBUG_BUILD=1`),
`unicode_hash` hits `assert(PyUnicode_CheckExact(o))` if an `istr`
subclass overrides `lower()` with a non-exact `str`.
- In release builds, casting a non-exact `str` to `PyASCIIObject*` risks
reading incorrect memory layouts.
- Subclassing `istr` is not intended in real-world usage; making `istr`
final simplifies the design and cleanly guarantees the canonical
identity invariant across the board.

### Changes Made:
1. **C Extension (`multidict/_multilib/istr.h`)**:
- Dropped `Py_TPFLAGS_BASETYPE` from `istr_spec` to forbid subclassing
`istr`.
2. **Pure Python (`multidict/_multidict_py.py`)**:
- Added `@final` decorator and `__init_subclass__` check raising
`TypeError: type 'multidict._multidict_py.istr' is not an acceptable
base type`.
- In `_CIMixin._identity()` and `_CSMixin._identity()`, ensure an exact
`str` is returned if a plain `str` subclass returns a non-exact `str`.
3. **Testing (`tests/test_istr.py`)**:
- Updated `test_subclass_ctor` to verify that attempting to subclass
`istr` raises `TypeError`.
- Added tests covering plain `str` subclasses overriding `lower()`
across both C and pure-Python backends.
   - 100% statement and branch coverage with zero CodeQL warnings.
4. **Towncrier Newsfragment**:
   - Updated `CHANGES/1535.bugfix.rst`.

## Verification:
- All tests pass in both C extension and pure-Python implementations
with 100% test coverage on changed files.
- Full test suite, sanitizers (ASan, TSan), CodeQL, and Hypothesis pass
in CI.
- C code formatted with `clang-format`, Python code formatted and linted
with `ruff`.

Keep one thread-local version counter on free-threaded builds (#1599)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

#1587 gave each thread a batch of versions in two thread-local
variables, `version_next` and `version_end`. Under the default TLS model
every access to a thread-local in a shared object goes through
`__tls_get_addr()`, and GCC recomputes the address rather than keep it
in a register, so each mutation made two such calls where it used to
make one `lock xadd`. On a single thread that cost about 34 instructions
per mutation.

A single `version_last` now does the job. A batch never hands out its
own base, a multiple of `VERSION_BATCH`, so reaching one means the batch
is spent, and starting the variable at `VERSION_BATCH - 1` makes the
first call refill. One `++version_last` reads and advances it, which is
one TLS lookup. Versions stay unique and increasing within a thread, the
same guarantees as before. The GIL build and the pure-Python
implementation are unaffected.

Instructions per operation, free-threaded 3.14.7t (Callgrind,
`benchmarks/callgrind_driver.py`):

| operation | `MultiDict` | `CIMultiDict` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `ctor_items` | 73,543 -> 70,308 (-4.4%) | 85,771 -> 82,536 (-3.8%) |
| `ctor_small` | 7,529 -> 7,175 (-4.7%) | 8,717 -> 8,363 (-4.1%) |
| `setitem_replace` | 527 -> 511 (-3.0%) | 584 -> 568 (-2.7%) |
| `setitem_insert` | 634 -> 617 (-2.6%) | 690 -> 674 (-2.4%) |
| `delitem` | 425 -> 409 (-3.8%) | 482 -> 466 (-3.3%) |
| `pop` | 565 -> 549 (-2.9%) | 622 -> 606 (-2.6%) |

Keep slot-level operations out of line (#1600)

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->

## What do these changes do?

`_multidict.c` and every `_multilib` header form one translation unit,
and GCC caps how much the whole unit may grow through inlining
(`inline-unit-growth`, 40%). `-fopt-info-inline` shows the cap refusing
98 call sites on the GIL build and 662 on the free-threaded one, so
unrelated edits keep moving these decisions (#1601 fixed one such case
on the insert path).

This marks `NOINLINE` the operations that sit behind Python slots
(`md_replace()`, `md_del()`, `md_repr()`) and the bulk update loops
(`md_update_from_dict/ht/seq()`, `md_extend_self()`). Otherwise they
compete with the hot paths for the budget, and freed budget goes to
inlining them into a slot such as `mp_ass_subscript`, where `delitem`
then pays `md_replace()`'s register saves. The bulk loops are refused
today anyway, so for them the attribute only pins the current layout.

It uses only the existing `NOINLINE` macro, which also works on MSVC,
with no build flags. The pure-Python implementation has nothing
equivalent.
